title: Capstone Part 3: Deployment, Communication, and Career Launch
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 3: Deployment, Communication, and Career Launch ##### Fourteen repositories, zero callbacks A candidate applying for data science roles in Bengaluru had a GitHub profile with fourteen repositories. Titanic. House prices. A Kaggle credit-card fraud notebook. An MNIST CNN. Each one a single `.ipynb` with the default filename, no README, and a final cell printing an accuracy score. He applied to sixty companies over four months. Three phone screens, no offers. He then deleted twelve of them. He kept one — an end-to-end forecasting project for a small kirana-supply distributor he had actually spoken to — and spent three weeks turning it into something else entirely: a README written as a case study, a tested pipeline, MLflow experiment logs, a Dockerized FastAPI service running on a ₹500-a-month VPS with a live URL, prediction logging, and a one-page executive summary that opened with "reduces stockouts by an estimated 22%, worth about ₹6.4 lakh a year for a distributor doing ₹3 crore in annual revenue." Six applications later he had two offers. Nothing about his modelling skill changed in those three weeks. What changed was that a hiring manager could, in ninety seconds, see a person who ships. Part 3 is that transformation, applied to your capstone. ##### From artifact to service Your Part 2 output is a pickled model and a validated number. Neither is a product. Deployment is the step that converts a file into something another system can call. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["MLflow model
registry"] --> B["FastAPI app
load at startup"] B --> C["Docker image
pinned deps"] C --> D["Container host
Cloud Run / ECS / VPS"] D --> E["/predict endpoint"] E --> F["Prediction log
request + output + version"] F --> G["Monitoring
drift + performance"] G -->|"trigger"| H["Retraining"] H --> A ``` The service itself, building on Day 36: ```python # app/main.py import os, time, json, logging, uuid from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from typing import Literal import mlflow.pyfunc, pandas as pd from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException from pydantic import BaseModel, Field MODEL_URI = os.environ["MODEL_URI"] # e.g. models:/coldchain-risk/Production MODEL_VERSION = os.getenv("MODEL_VERSION", "unknown") logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s") pred_log = logging.getLogger("predictions") state: dict = {} @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): state["model"] = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(MODEL_URI) # load once, not per request yield state.clear() app = FastAPI(title="Cold-chain spoilage risk", version=MODEL_VERSION, lifespan=lifespan) class Shipment(BaseModel): route_id: str = Field(..., pattern=r"^RT-\d{5}$") vehicle_type: Literal["reefer_small", "reefer_large", "insulated_van"] box_sku: str load_kg: float = Field(..., gt=0, le=900) planned_transit_hours: float = Field(..., gt=0, le=96) forecast_max_temp_c: float = Field(..., ge=-5, le=52) dispatch_hour_ist: int = Field(..., ge=0, le=23) class Prediction(BaseModel): request_id: str spoilage_probability: float recommend_upgrade: bool model_version: str latency_ms: float THRESHOLD = float(os.getenv("DECISION_THRESHOLD", "0.34")) # from the Part 2 cost analysis @app.get("/health") def health(): return {"status": "ok", "model_version": MODEL_VERSION} @app.post("/predict", response_model=Prediction) def predict(shipment: Shipment): t0 = time.perf_counter() rid = str(uuid.uuid4()) try: X = pd.DataFrame([shipment.model_dump()]) p = float(state["model"].predict(X)[0]) except Exception as exc: logging.exception("inference failed") raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="inference error") from exc latency = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 pred_log.info(json.dumps({ "request_id": rid, "ts": time.time(), "model_version": MODEL_VERSION, "features": shipment.model_dump(), "prediction": p, "latency_ms": latency, })) return Prediction( request_id=rid, spoilage_probability=round(p, 4), recommend_upgrade=p >= THRESHOLD, model_version=MODEL_VERSION, latency_ms=round(latency, 2), ) ``` Four production details worth naming. The model loads **once at startup** via the lifespan handler, not per request. Pydantic validates inputs at the boundary, so a malformed payload returns a 422 rather than a confusing traceback. Every prediction is logged as structured JSON with a request ID and model version — that log is the raw material for monitoring, and without it you are blind. And the threshold is an environment variable, because the business will want to tune the flag rate without a redeploy. ```dockerfile FROM python:3.11-slim AS base ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 WORKDIR /app RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libgomp1 \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY app/ ./app/ RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser && chown -R appuser /app USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s \ CMD python -c "import urllib.request;urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health')" CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"] ``` `libgomp1` is there because LightGBM needs it and slim images do not ship it — a twenty-minute debugging session you can now skip. The non-root user and healthcheck are what separate a demo container from a deployable one. ##### Monitoring and the retraining plan Day 38 covered drift detection in depth. For the capstone, the deliverable is a **written plan**, not a full observability stack. One page answering: | Question | Your answer should look like | |---|---| | What do you log? | Every request: features, prediction, model version, timestamp, request ID | | When do labels arrive? | Spoilage confirmed at delivery, 6–72 hours later, joined nightly on shipment_id | | What do you watch? | PSI per feature (weekly), prediction-mean shift (daily), recall@15% (weekly, once labels land) | | What thresholds alert? | PSI > 0.2 on any top-10 feature; recall drops > 5 points below the 0.58 baseline | | Who is paged? | Named owner, with a runbook link | | What triggers a retrain? | Scheduled monthly, or immediately on a sustained 2-week recall breach | | How do you roll back? | Previous model version stays in the registry; flip `MODEL_URI` and redeploy | Paleyes et al.'s 2022 survey of ML deployment case studies found that the recurring failures are organisational — unclear ownership, no monitoring, no rollback path — far more than algorithmic. Writing this table is a stronger portfolio signal than another 0.01 of AUC. ##### The write-up that people actually read Apply Day 41's storytelling discipline to your own project. Your README's first screen is the whole pitch. Structure it like this: 1. **One-line description and a live link.** "Predicts cold-chain spoilage risk at dispatch so ops can upgrade packaging. Live demo: `https://…/docs`." 2. **Executive summary — one paragraph.** Problem, approach, result, impact in rupees or units. This is the paragraph a recruiter reads. 3. **One chart.** The single visual that carries the finding, embedded as an image. 4. **Problem framing.** Decision, decision point, target definition, metric — from Part 1. 5. **Data and pipeline.** Sources, volume, period, how to reproduce. 6. **Modelling.** The ladder table with metrics, the winner, and why. 7. **Validation.** Split strategy, honest test number with a confidence interval. 8. **Interpretation and error analysis.** SHAP plot and the failure mode you found. 9. **Deployment.** Architecture diagram, endpoint docs, latency. 10. **Monitoring and retraining.** The table above. 11. **Limitations.** Written honestly. This section builds more credibility than any other. 12. **Reproduce it.** `make setup && make train && make serve`. A worked executive summary, so you can see the shape: > Cold-chain shipments of temperature-sensitive pharma spoil at a rate of 3.1%, costing the distributor roughly ₹1.9 crore a year. Existing practice flags all monsoon-season routes for premium packaging, catching 41% of spoilage while upgrading 22% of shipments. This project predicts spoilage risk at dispatch using only route, vehicle, load, and weather-forecast features, reaching 61% recall at a 15% flag rate on a time-forward test set of 18,400 shipments (95% CI 57–65%). Applied at current volumes, that is an estimated ₹1.2 crore of avoided loss with one-third fewer packaging upgrades. The model is deployed as a Dockerized FastAPI service with p95 latency of 34 ms, logs every prediction for drift monitoring, and is scheduled for monthly retraining. Nine sentences. Problem, cost, baseline, method, result with uncertainty, impact, deployment status. That paragraph does more for your candidacy than the whole notebook underneath it. ##### Portfolio: quality over volume The hiring signal is not "can this person fit a model" — libraries do that. It is "can this person take an ambiguous problem to a working, maintained system and explain it." So: **two or three deep projects, not fourteen shallow ones.** Delete the Titanic notebook. Genuinely delete it. What makes a repo credible: - **A real or realistic problem**, ideally with a named stakeholder — a local business, an NGO, an open civic dataset from `data.gov.in`, your college's operations. Kaggle datasets are acceptable; Kaggle *problems* (pre-cleaned, pre-framed) are not, because framing is the skill being assessed. - **Commit history that shows iteration**, not one commit called "final". - **Tests.** Even five. Almost no candidate portfolio has them, so they are disproportionately noticed. - **A live endpoint.** A free Cloud Run instance or a small VPS. Being clickable is worth more than being correct. - **A clean `requirements.txt` or lockfile** and a README that runs on someone else's machine. - **Honest limitations.** Overclaiming is the fastest way to fail a technical interview; a candidate who says "this is observational and I'd want a randomised rollout to confirm" reads as senior. Add a short slide deck or a five-minute Loom walkthrough. Many hiring managers will watch a five-minute video who would never clone a repo. ##### Interviewing on your own work The capstone walkthrough is the highest-leverage interview asset you have, because you control the ground. Rehearse a **five-minute version** with this timing: - **0:00–0:45 — Business problem.** Who hurts, how much it costs, what decision is being made. - **0:45–1:30 — Framing.** Target definition, decision point, metric and why, baseline. - **1:30–3:00 — Technical decisions.** Two or three, each stated as a choice with alternatives and a reason. "I used a grouped time-forward split because the same route recurs and a random split leaked route history — that took the estimate from 0.91 to 0.87, and the 0.87 is the one that held." - **3:00–4:00 — Results and impact.** The honest number with its interval, translated to rupees or units. - **4:00–5:00 — Limitations and what's next.** One real weakness and a concrete plan. Then prepare for the follow-ups, which are predictable: - "How do you know it isn't overfitting?" → split strategy, nested CV or once-touched test set, the gap between selection and test scores. - "What would you do with three more months?" → shows product thinking. - "Why not deep learning?" → the ladder, and the gap between rungs. - "How would this fail in production?" → drift, the feedback loop, the segment where recall is weak. - "What did you get wrong?" → have a real answer ready. Everyone has one; candidates who claim otherwise are not believed. On strategy: apply to fewer companies with tailored material rather than mass-applying. Referrals convert at several times the rate of cold applications, so spend time in communities — local PyData and Kaggle meetups in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad — writing about what you built. A blog post explaining one hard decision from your capstone doubles as a portfolio piece and an interview rehearsal. ##### Common mistakes - A portfolio of tutorial notebooks with no framing, deployment, or write-up. - No README, or a README that is just installation commands. - Reporting accuracy with no baseline and no business translation. - A model that only runs on your machine with unpinned dependencies. - Loading the model inside the request handler instead of at startup. - No prediction logging, making post-deployment monitoring impossible. - Running the container as root and hardcoding secrets in the image. - Hiding limitations, which reads as either dishonesty or inexperience. - A twenty-minute walkthrough when you were asked for five. - Describing what you did without ever saying what you *chose* and why. - Fourteen repositories where two would be stronger. ##### Hands-on: finish and publish Your practical task is the deployment plus the summary: Dockerized FastAPI service, documented endpoint, prediction logging, a drift and retraining note, and the one-page executive summary. Get the container running on a real host today, even a free tier — a URL you can paste into an application changes how your work is received. The mini project is publication: the clean repository with pipeline, tracked experiments, deployed service, tests, and a README written as a case study, plus a short presentation. Ask someone outside data science to read the first screen of your README and tell you what the project does and why it matters. If they cannot, rewrite the executive summary — the code is not the problem. The assignment is rehearsal. Record yourself doing the five-minute walkthrough. Watch it once, which is unpleasant and useful. You will hear yourself explaining what you did rather than what you decided, and you will hear the moment you drift past five minutes. Re-record until the business problem is clear in forty-five seconds and every technical claim has a "because" attached to it. ##### Key takeaways - **Deployment is what turns an artifact into evidence** — a Dockerized service with a live URL, structured prediction logging, and versioned models is the difference between a notebook and a system. - **Write the monitoring and retraining plan even for a portfolio project**; the recurring failures in real ML deployments are organisational, and showing you know that marks you as production-minded. - **Your README is the deliverable most people will actually consume.** Lead with a quantified executive summary and one well-chosen chart. - **Two or three deep, honest projects beat fourteen tutorials.** Real problem, iteration history, tests, live endpoint, and a limitations section you actually wrote. - **Rehearse the five-minute walkthrough** framed as decisions with reasons — that narrative, not the AUC, is what gets you the offer.
